rewrites.blindSummary: This country is workable — its region's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside its top legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; cities host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit gender-identity protections and no legal-gender-recognition statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex relations legal and employment discrimination prohibited — no partner-related exposure for visitors.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: No explicit gender-identity protections and no legal-gender-recognition statute (administrative practice unclear) — resident-facing gaps.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Legal-gender-recognition statute absent; evidence base thin but consistent.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations are not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex-union recognition; LGBTIQ organisations register freely; the first public pride was held in 2013, only the second in its region; polls from 2019 to 2021 found most residents would accept a homosexual neighbour; this country is one of two UN LGBTI core-group members in its region and made 2024 universal-periodic-review anti-discrimination commitments.

Human-rights database (20 July 2018): the 2018 pride week, held in the capital, featured a parade plus NGO campaigns — local organisations petitioning the national legislature for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; a national gender-equality institute and a UN women's body were engaged.

News agency report (11 July 2017): the head of government said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from a governing-party secretary-general's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Regional survey organisation dispatch (May 2020): respondents in the region are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; this country stood out with two regional peers as particularly tolerant; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Media interview (22 June 2016) with a trans woman who came out in the late 1990s: she described this country as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other countries in its region, but reported verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2012; small, peaceful, with growing tourism; no legal gender recognition; no documented anti-trans violence; a thin community.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2012 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
blindSourceSummaries: Online legal reference summary: same-sex conduct legal since 2012; a 2021 law set an equal age of consent of 18 (previously 16); no relationship recognition or adoption; the 2019 labour code bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition.

Online reference summary: under the penal code in force since November 2012 same-sex conduct is legal with an equal age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity; the 2019 labour code bans workplace discrimination on sexual orientation; penal-code provisions allow enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred; no same-sex marriages, civil unions or partnerships are recognised; a 2016 poll found fewer than half of residents would not mind an LGBTQ neighbour.

Online reference page (updated 25 April 2026): same-sex conduct legal since the November 2012 penal code with an equal age of consent of 16; no recognition of same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships; the page lists no general anti-discrimination protection (the 2019 labour-code employment ban is not reflected there); records this country among signatories of a UN joint statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the penal code and religious-law framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming people face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 human-rights shadow report documents violations of an international human-rights covenant). BUT: the tourist resorts operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted at a resort; the risk concentrates in the capital and local areas.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local contact raises it.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 8 years, 100 lashes available) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners, and the operative law in any local area.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Resorts are de-facto insulated; the score reflects the national legal framework and local exposure.
blindSourceSummaries: Human-rights measurement organisation summary report 2024 (second expert survey): human-rights experts most commonly identified LGBTQIA+ people — alongside migrants, human-rights defenders, journalists, religious minorities and sex workers — as at risk of empowerment-rights violations; political-participation scores were relatively better while other civil and political rights scored considerably lower.

Human-rights journalism outlet (1 September 2015): police arrested two men on 29 August for homosexual activity in their private home; the 2014 penal code extended criminalisation beyond followers of the national religion to everyone, with death-penalty provisions theoretically in reach; a local LGBT-rights organisation warned tourists could face similar threats.

UN human-rights office compilation (March 2015) for this country's second-cycle universal periodic review: records reservations and concerns under international human-rights covenants, including religious-law-based treatment of children born outside marriage; an international human-rights body recommended anti-discrimination legislation covering sexual orientation and action against stigmatisation of homosexuals.

This country's national universal periodic review report (April 2015), the government's own submission: of more than 100 first-cycle recommendations it fully accepted the large majority, partially accepted some, took note of a few and rejected others with reasons; it reports full implementation of many and partial implementation of others over four years.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is workable for trans visitors — its region's strongest legal framework on paper. The constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; a 2015 anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; legal gender recognition is possible (medicalised); and the government attempted same-sex unions in 2024 as part of accession to a regional body. Counterweights: implementation is inconsistent, political hate speech is common (a 2022 report found the year marked by intolerance), and the capital's pride proceeds under protection.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2024 same-sex unions attempt — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners; not yet law.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The medicalised legal gender recognition process is resident-facing; the implementation gaps affect resident victims.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: De jure unit: scored separately from a neighbouring nation per boundaries. Implementation gaps are resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation overview (updated March 2026): a constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination plus a 2015 anti-discrimination law covering gender identity — but implementation inconsistent; the head of government's April 2024 pledge to legalise same-sex civil unions stalled, and as of February 2026 parliament had still failed to adopt the new civil code amid fierce opposition, including from the ruling party.
Source note: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying newswire report (May 2024) covers this country considering same-sex unions amid fierce opposition.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: the head of government pledged during pride week to get the civil code adopted (in 2022 parliament had voted against same-sex-couple recognition amendments); a justice-ministry working group was drafting a bill; a local civil-society organisation's 2022 annual report found intolerance and hatred, with politicians' hate speech common during civil-code debates; an artist received death threats over a painting; the pride week was held under its own slogan.

Regional news outlet (January 2019): a regional human-rights court ruled that a neighbouring country's surgery requirement for gender-marker change violates private-life rights; a local person with a case before the national top court on name and gender change on national identity documents watched the ruling closely, documenting that this country's legal gender recognition route ran through the courts at that time.
News outlet (March 2022): this country's parliament rejected the new law recognising same-sex civil unions (the page was largely navigation content at fetch time).

Regional news outlet: the third annual pride parade in the capital, with week-long exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions by a local equality organisation (its slogan both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade); visible, public LGBTI organising in the capital.
Business news outlet: analysis of the new civil code's gender-neutral marriage language and its implications for same-sex marriage (the page was largely navigation content at fetch time).

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community.
rewrites.blindTangential: The criminal code criminalises same-sex conduct, the 2014 amendment added an 'aggravated homosexuality' offence (life imprisonment for 'serial offenders'), and in 2024 the national legislature raised the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to 5 years — the trajectory is towards harsher penalties, not reform. Under the previous leader, LGBTI people faced documented persecution, including his infamous rhetoric; the current government era has seen some improvement in general freedoms but no decriminalisation and continued severe discrimination (a human-rights organisation). Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country profile (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised since the historic era; the 2014 'aggravated homosexuality' life clause was removed by the March 2025 criminal code, which instead sets a five-year minimum for 'unnatural offences' (defined as any homosexual act) with no stated maximum, plus three years for 'gross indecency'; the current government has not typically enforced the provisions.
Regional radio outlet: reports this country's new criminal-law package raising the minimum sentence for homosexual acts to five years — broadcast corroboration of the penalty change now on the books.

Human-rights monitoring organisation annual report 2024: this country rated partly free; political freedoms improved under the current government after two decades of the previous leader's rule, with severe discrimination against LGBT+ people listed among ongoing concerns.

Foreign government's country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in this country (February 2023): systematic assessment of risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information on law and treatment — among the fullest documentation of conditions on the ground.

Human-rights organisation report (September 2015): arbitrary arrests, torture and killings in this country under the previous leader, including his anti-gay rhetoric and explicit threats against LGBT people — the enforcement climate of the previous regime, relevant to how police treat visibly LGBT visitors.
Foreign government's 2020 human-rights report on this country: same-sex conduct criminalised (up to life under the 2013 amendment); documents arrests and societal discrimination.
Foreign government's 2021 report: continued criminalisation with no prosecutions reported; significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This state/province carries the country's strictest criminalised restroom regime. Its 2026 facility-use law, effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching their birth sex — in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants and hospitals — with a misdemeanour of up to one year and a felony of up to five years on a repeat within five years. Four successive legislative rounds ran from 2023 to 2026, alongside a ban on official recognition of Pride flags.

A lawsuit in the national courts followed the law's passage; contemporaneous reporting states the law was partially blocked, leaving it in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Since then a March 2026 bill extending felony restroom penalties to all public accommodations has passed the lower chamber, a March 2026 forced-outing statute has been signed, a birth-marker freeze has been in effect since January 2026, and the nation's Supreme Court declined in 2024 to review the state/province's bar on gender-affirming care.
rewrites.blindTangential: Four successive legislative rounds (2023-2026) targeted LGBT+ rights broadly - the pride-flag ban reaches symbols rather than trans presence directly.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: Birth-certificate and ID marker rules follow the national sex-registration framework; changing them is resident-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: Local civil-liberties organisation on the 2026 facility-use bill: signed by the governor, effective 1 July 2026; makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching birth sex — in government buildings and any public-facing private business (gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues, hospitals); first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to a year in jail. The organisation filed suit on 30 April 2026 arguing due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations, noting the law targets no actual criminal conduct.

Source note: page not retrievable at fetch time (wire service blocks automated fetch); the underlying national-wire article covers the legislature passing the transgender bathroom ban and jail threats, and the lawsuit that partially blocked it.

National news outlet with a local news partner (30 April 2026): six transgender residents sued to block the law before its 1 July 2026 effect; the law is the only state/province law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses and carries steeper penalties than comparable laws elsewhere (per a civil-liberties organisation); the suit challenges the bill as unconstitutional.
